'''Wylie Walker Vale Jr.''' (July 3, 1941 – January 3, 2012) was an American endocrinologist who helped identify hormones controlling basic bodily functions.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Evans | first1 = R. | author-link = Ronald M. Evans| title = Wylie Walker Vale Jr (1941–2012) | doi = 10.1038/483542a | journal = Nature | volume = 483 | issue = 7391 | pages = 542 | year = 2012 | pmid =  22460892| bibcode = 2012Natur.483..542E | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Stenvers | first1 = K. L. | last2 = Findlay | first2 = J. K. | title = Inhibins and activins: Towards the future. A tribute to the late Professor Wylie W. Vale | doi = 10.1016/j.mce.2012.03.001 | journal = Molecular and Cellular Endocrinology | year = 2012 | pmid = 22406753 | volume=359 | issue=1–2 | pages=1| s2cid = 37455861 }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Vale was born in Houston, Texas, on July 3, 1941. He completed a B.A. degree in biology at [[Rice University]] and obtained a Ph.D. in [[physiology]] and [[biochemistry]] from [[Baylor College of Medicine]]. He commenced employment at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] in [[San Diego]], [[California]], in 1970.<ref name=salkobit/>

==Career==
In collaboration with his advisor and mentor [[Roger Guillemin]], Vale contributed to the discovery, isolation and identification of [[thyrotropin releasing hormone]] and [[gonadotropin-releasing hormone]] in the 1970s;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lemke |first1=Greg |title=Roger Guillemin (1924–2024), neuroscientist who showed how the brain controls hormones |journal=Nature |date=8 March 2024 |volume=627 |issue=8003 |pages=266 |doi=10.1038/d41586-024-00714-4 |pmid=38459135 |bibcode=2024Natur.627..266L |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00714-4 |access-date=14 July 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=nytimes>{{cite news |last1=Wade |first1=Nicholas |author1-link=Nicholas Wade |title=Roger Guillemin, 100, Nobel-Winning Scientist Stirred by Rivalries, Dies |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/02/22/science/roger-guillemin-dead.html |work=The New York Times |date=23 February 2024}}</ref> work that led to the [[Nobel Prize]] for Guillemin.<ref name=mclellan2012wp/>

At the Salk Institute, Vale led efforts in identifying the group of hormones involved in human growth, reproduction and temperature.<ref name=ntimesobit>{{cite news | last = Wade| first = Nicholas| title = Wylie Vale Jr., Groundbreaking Endocrinologist, Dies at 70| newspaper = The New York Times| date = January 15, 2012| url = https://www.nytimes.com/2012/01/16/science/wylie-vale-jr-groundbreaking-endocrinologist-dies-at-70.html?_r=1&hpw| access-date = 2012-01-16}}</ref> His group discovered, isolated and identified  [[corticotropin-releasing hormone]] (CRF/CRH) in 1981 and [[growth hormone releasing factor]] (GHRF) in 1982.<ref name=mclellan2012wp/>

Vale also founded two [[biotechnology company|biotechnology companies]], [[Neurocrine Biosciences]] and [[Acceleron Pharma]].<ref name=mclellan2012wp>{{Citation |last=McLellan |first=Dennis |date=January 20, 2012
 |title=Wylie W. Vale Jr., who made critical discoveries in brain chemistry, dies |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]
 |at=washingtonpost.com |access-date=2012-01-21 |format=reprint ([[Los Angeles Times]] original)
 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/science/wylie-w-vale-jr-who-made-critical-discoveries-in-brain-chemistry-dies/2012/01/18/gIQA7uNrEQ_story.html }}</ref>

Vale was head of both the Clayton Foundation Laboratories for Peptide Biology and the Helen McLoraine Chair in Molecular Neurobiology at the Salk Institute.<ref name=salkobit/> He died in 2012.<ref name=salkobit>{{cite press release| title = Wylie Vale, Salk scientist, pioneer and leader, dies at 70| publisher = Salk Institute| date = January 6, 2012| url = http://www.salk.edu/news/pressrelease_details.php?press_id=535| access-date = 2012-01-16}}</ref>
